content.p: The Aryan Brotherhood is one of the oldest and best-known racist prison gangs in the United States. It began in California's San Quentin prison in 1964 and, according to prosecutors and journalists, grew from a small clique of white inmates into a network that spread through state and federal prisons and out onto the streets. Its members call it the Brand. Its motto, "blood in, blood out", describes the price of entry, which was often an attack on another prisoner, and the price of leaving, which was death.

Its history has been written largely from three kinds of evidence: the accounts of former members, the words of prosecutors, and court verdicts. They do not always agree. In the 2006 trial, defence lawyers argued that the men in the dock were ageing prisoners who had banded together to survive, and that the government's case rested on paid informants. The jury convicted all four defendants, and a second jury in 2024 convicted three more leaders. Nearly every figure for the gang's size, its murders and its reach comes from one side or the other, and this account attributes each one.

The gang was founded in 1964 at San Quentin State Prison, according to a civil-rights monitoring group's extremist file on the gang. That group is cited below as the monitoring group. Prison officials were then beginning to desegregate state and federal prisons, and black and white inmates were thrown together, often for the first time. The original members were largely Irish bikers who called themselves the Diamond Tooth Gang, because they wore shards of glass in their teeth. After merging with other white cliques in the prison they took the name Aryan Brotherhood.

The New Yorker, in a 2004 investigation by David Grann, described the same yard in similar terms. White inmates, mostly bikers along with a few neo-Nazis, decided to strike at Black prisoners who were organising the Black Guerrilla Family under the influence of the prison leader George Jackson. Violence of this kind was new even at San Quentin, which inmates called "gladiator school". The novelist Edward Bunker, who was an inmate at the time, told the magazine that everything was seen through the lens of race.

The gang spread quickly through the California system. By 1975 it had reached most state prisons, where the authorities say a full race war was under way, and dozens of inmates had already died. Within about two more years, as senior members were transferred to federal prisons, the gang began to put down roots there as well. It split into a California branch and a federal branch, which the monitoring group quoted one former top leader as calling "two related but different crime families". The monitoring group says fewer than 100 members belonged in the late 1970s. According to the monitoring group, the gang also signed a truce with the Mexican Mafia, a Latino prison gang, during the Mexican Mafia's war with La Nuestra Familia. It reads the truce as early evidence that the Brotherhood cared more about profit than ideological purity.

Where other prison gangs recruited the newest and most vulnerable inmates, the Brotherhood, according to the New Yorker's review of FBI reports, prison records and court documents, took only the most capable and violent. Each recruit had to "make his bones", which commonly meant killing another prisoner. The monitoring group adds that attacking a rival or assaulting a corrections officer could also serve. Members swore the "blood in, blood out" oath.

The symbols are well documented. An anti-extremism group's database of hate symbols says the shamrock, often paired with a swastika, is the most common emblem, and that members also use the letters AB, the numbers 1 and 2, and 666. Michael Thompson, a former high-ranking member interviewed by the New Yorker, described being tattooed with a shamrock on his hand.

Thompson told the magazine that recruits were handed books: Sun Tzu's The Art of War, Machiavelli's The Prince and Nietzsche. The gang's nickname came from the western novels of Louis L'Amour, whose gunslingers ride for "the brand". The monitoring group says inductees were also required to read Hitler's Mein Kampf, and that many members follow Asatru, a modern revival of Norse paganism.
content.h2: From a mob to a council
content.p: In the early years the gang ran on a "one man, one vote" rule. The monitoring group says that by the early 1980s the arrangement was causing chaos. An internal California corrections report, as the New Yorker described it, predicted that the gang would not pose a serious threat to law enforcement unless it gained a clear chain of command.

Thompson told the magazine that this was what he and other leaders set out to build. He wanted "to eliminate the irrationality and make it into a true organized-crime family", he said. The New Yorker reported that gang members awaiting trial at a prison in Chino acted as their own lawyers and subpoenaed associates from across the country, which let much of the gang meet in the yard for days. Out of that gathering came a structure modelled loosely on the Italian Mafia. A council of about a dozen members, chosen by majority vote, would run the state system, with a three-man commission above it. A similar hierarchy was set up in the federal prisons. According to the monitoring group, Thompson served on the California council, while Barry Mills, Tyler "T.D." Bingham and John Greschner, who quit in 1999 and later talked to investigators, oversaw the federal side.

The New Yorker reported that the gang also adopted a policy of reaching a witness's family when the witness himself was out of reach. Thompson said the killing of an informant's father and of a young woman in 1982 was what made him leave. According to the magazine, Thompson became the highest-ranking defector in the gang's history and testified against the man later convicted of the two murders. Thompson told the writer that the Brotherhood "is not about white supremacy" but "about supremacy". The monitoring group describes the gang as above all a criminal enterprise, and its quotation from former leader Michael Thompson reads: "Is there racism? You bet there's racism. Is it dominant? No."

The attack that Slate credits with reshaping American prisons came in federal custody. At the U.S. Penitentiary at Marion, Illinois, Thomas Silverstein and Clayton Fountain, both identified by the monitoring group as Aryan Brotherhood members, were already known to the authorities. Slate reported that in 1981 the pair were charged with murder over the death of an inmate, Robert Chappelle, who was Black, in the control unit. Prison reporter Pete Earley, quoted by Slate, said the two later killed Raymond "Cadillac" Smith, stabbing him 67 times and dragging his body along the tier. The monitoring group's 2005 report says the 67-stab victim was the leader of a rival gang, the D.C. Blacks.

On the morning of 22 October 1983, the Bureau of Prisons says, Silverstein was being escorted from a shower back to his cell in the control unit when he broke away. Another inmate freed him from his restraints and handed him a knife. Silverstein attacked Officer Merle E. Clutts, who died of his wounds, and then surrendered. Slate says Clutts was stabbed about 40 times and puts the time of Fountain's separate attack on a second officer, Robert Hoffman, a few hours later. Slate describes that attack as fatal. The monitoring group says only that Fountain stabbed Hoffman and assaulted two other officers.

The consequences outlasted both men. Marion went into lockdown within days and stayed there for 23 years. Slate argues that the lockdown became the model for later "supermax" prisons across the country, including ADX Florence in Colorado. Human rights groups criticised the isolation; Amnesty International said in 1987 that there was hardly a rule in the United Nations minimum standards that Marion did not infringe in some way. A former federal prisons director, Norman Carlson, defended the policy, telling the San Francisco Chronicle in 1998 that for men with multiple life sentences another life sentence was no deterrent. Slate says inmate murders and assaults at Marion fell sharply afterwards.

Slate reported in 2013 that Silverstein had been held in solitary confinement since 1983. The Bureau of Prisons says he died on 11 May 2019 at a hospital while serving his sentence at the federal prison in Florence, Colorado. Fountain died in his cell in 2004, Slate reported, after becoming a lay member of a Trappist monastic order.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Gregory Jessner began looking into the gang in 1992, after a convicted murderer was found strangled in his cell at the federal prison in Lompoc, California, the New Yorker reported. He found that so few of the gang's crimes were ever prosecuted that there were no reliable statistics on them. By the 1990s the authorities had moved nearly all the leaders into supermax prisons, where they were locked down almost all day. The gang still found ways to pass orders, according to the New Yorker and the monitoring group's 2005 report: tapping Morse code, whispering through vents, using women on the outside as couriers, and writing in invisible ink made from urine.

The anti-extremism group and NPR both describe the use of those messages at trial. The most serious episode prosecutors pointed to followed an outbreak of racial violence at Marion in 1997. The monitoring group's 2005 report says the indictment alleged the leaders issued a "formal declaration of war" on Black inmates throughout the federal system, using coded calls and a double alphabet invented in 1623 by Sir Francis Bacon. Two Black inmates at the federal prison at Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, were then killed and four wounded. The New Yorker said investigators decoded a note from Bingham only after the two men had been found dead in their cells, one stabbed 34 times and the other 35. Defence lawyers said a recorded call played at trial showed members warning one another about rising tension, not planning attacks.

On 28 August 2002 a federal grand jury indicted what the New Yorker called virtually the entire suspected leadership of the gang. The charges covered stabbings, strangulations, poisonings, contract killings, extortion, robbery and drug trafficking. That report counted 40 members and associates among the defendants, 21 of them eligible for the death penalty, and described it as the biggest death penalty prosecution the US courts had seen. The indictment alleged that gang members either carried out or solicited 32 murders and attempted murders over about 25 years.

U.S. marshals made the arrests in December 2002 in one coordinated operation. The New Yorker described agents taking inmates from Pelican Bay in California, a prison in New Hampshire, a jail in Sacramento and the federal supermax at Florence, and flying most of the 40 people seized to Los Angeles. Besides inmates, the group included five women on the outside, three former convicts and a former prison guard.

The first trial, in Santa Ana, California, began in March 2006 against Mills, Bingham, Christopher Gibson and Edgar Hevle. NPR reported that prosecutors had spent four months laying out a case built on years of intercepted mail and screened phone calls. Prosecutors sought the death penalty against Mills and Bingham. The jury heard recorded calls, saw prison-yard video and was shown coded messages.

The defence argued that the government's witnesses were informants with reasons to lie. Mills's lawyer, Mark Fleming, said many had been held together in a unit at the federal prison in Florence with access to files and a computer, so that agreement between them proved nothing. NPR also reported that an informant, Danny Weeks, who was not called to testify, described the unit as comfortable. Prosecutors said dozens of witnesses had corroborated each violent act.

On 28 July 2006, after two weeks of deliberation, jurors convicted Mills and Bingham of ordering attacks on Black inmates from their cells. The anti-extremism group reported that Gibson and Hevle were convicted of conspiring to murder Black inmates. NPR said the case required jurors to answer nearly 80 questions. In September the penalty phase ended in deadlock. JURIST reported that U.S. District Judge David O. Carter declared a mistrial on the death penalty after four and a half days of jury discussion, leaving Mills and Bingham to serve life in prison without parole. By that group's count in August 2006, of the 40 members originally charged, 19 had reached plea bargains and one had died.

Barry Byron Mills, known as the Baron, was 21 when he was convicted of armed robbery in 1969 and sent to San Quentin, the monitoring group reported. He was found dead in the cellblocks of the federal supermax in Florence, Colorado, one day after his 70th birthday in July 2018. The Fremont County coroner said his death did not appear suspicious and that he seemingly died of natural causes, pending an autopsy. In a 2012 interview with the monitoring group's Intelligence Report, another founding member credited Mills with turning a state-prison gang of 50 to 60 members into one of more than 20,000, a figure the monitoring group reported on that account.

The Brotherhood did not disappear after 2006. In April 2024 a federal jury in Sacramento found Ronald "Renegade" Yandell, Danny Troxell and William Sylvester guilty of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to murder, after a trial that lasted nearly three months, a Bay Area newspaper reported. Yandell was also convicted of drug distribution. Evidence included a two-month wiretap run by the Drug Enforcement Administration, along with inmate-made knives and bags of drugs.

The cases that came out of the trial turned partly on a 2015 killing at California State Prison, Sacramento. CBS News San Francisco, citing court records and the U.S. Attorney's Office, reported that Yandell was convicted of ordering two inmates to kill Hugo Pinell, a Black Guerrilla Family member who was one of the "San Quentin Six", offering them membership in return. The U.S. Attorney's Office said the DEA later intercepted calls in which Yandell bragged of directing the killing. The same newspaper said California's corrections chief, Jeffrey Macomber, testified as a defence witness that officials had been warned more than once that putting Pinell on a general-population yard would get him killed, though he said they also had conflicting information.

Sylvester was convicted of murdering another inmate to earn membership. His lawyer argued that the motive was dislike of a "known child molester", not gang business. Troxell's lawyer portrayed him as a peacemaker who called off murders. Yandell's defence accused officials of retaliating against him for his role in a prisoner hunger strike against solitary confinement. The newspaper also reported that defence lawyers found an email from the DEA case agent saying he wanted to "crush him so bad my teeth hurt", and made it the centrepiece of a motion to dismiss the case for vindictive prosecution.

In December 2024 Judge Kimberly Mueller sentenced Yandell, then 62, and Sylvester, then 56, to consecutive life terms, CBS reported. Yandell denied the crimes at his sentencing, and his lawyer said he would appeal. The newspaper later reported that eight members were sentenced to federal prison in 2025 after two trials, and that federal prosecutors in Northern California had charged dozens of members and associates since 2019.

On 23 October 2025 an Aryan Brotherhood member, Todd "Fox" Morgan, 57, was killed with improvised weapons on the yard at Salinas Valley State Prison, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, as reported by that newspaper. The department named three inmates as suspects: Todd Givens, Ray Waldron and Robert England. They had been moved to restrictive housing and no motive had been released. Court filings from January 2024 had named England as an inmate the gang allegedly wanted dead, over a note attributed to member Pat Brady. Morgan was serving a federal sentence tied to a 2020 indictment of the Aryan Brotherhood and other white groups.

The gang's real size remains uncertain. The New Yorker in 2004 put its core at about a hundred members, all convicted felons. The monitoring group says officials estimate about 20,000, and CBS in 2024 cited estimates of 15,000 to 20,000 members both inside and outside prison. The FBI, as reported in the monitoring group's 2005 report, attributed 18 percent of all prison murders to the gang, though it makes up less than a tenth of one percent of inmates. The anti-extremism group cautions that other groups using the Aryan Brotherhood name, such as the Aryan Brotherhood of Texas, are independent and unrelated to the original.
